about: Part of the reference catalogue: designed experiments from one published source, for testing that software reproduces them.
source: the citation, with what was read and when. experiments: each with its data (factors, responses, runs
exactly as printed, in the printed order), where it is printed, and expected: every number the source prints for
it, as printed text, with what it is, where it is printed (a line or page, and a quotation) and check: how to
recompute it (the kind of result, the term, the model in the library's formula notation, and runs, the 1-based
positions of the runs used when not all), or manual, the reason it is not recomputed. designs: designs without
responses, with the properties the source states. Read with process_improve.experiments.reference_catalogue.
reference_experiments; tests/test_reference_catalogue.py recomputes every number that has a check.

source.title: Response Surfaces, Mixtures, and Ridge Analyses
source.pages: front matter, pp. v to xiv, chapters 1 to 20, pp. 1 to 628, the answers to the exercises, pp. 629 to 742, and the tables, bibliography and indexes, pp. 743 to 857
source.publisher: Wiley-Interscience, John Wiley & Sons, Hoboken, New Jersey
source.cite: Box, G. E. P. and Draper, N. R. (2007), Response Surfaces, Mixtures, and Ridge Analyses, 2nd edition, Wiley
source.read: 2026-10-24, the whole book, from the front matter to p. 857. The tables of pp. 743 to 756 (normal, t, F and chi-square) are not recorded: they are tables of distributions, not experiments. The bibliography and the indexes hold no numbers to record
source.rights: The book is protected by copyright (© 2007 John Wiley & Sons, Inc.) and is not reproduced here. This file holds facts it reports (numbers, layouts, data) and short quotations that locate each one, for citation and for checking software. The MIT licence of process-improve does not extend to them.

designs.name: box-draper-2-consecutive-reaction-theoretical-surface
designs.title: A theoretical yield surface of a consecutive reaction A -> B -> C, graduated locally by a plane in region R1

design.type: a theoretical response function in reaction time (h) and temperature (K), printed without data

designs.notes: The yield of the intermediate B, Eq. (2A.1), with rate constants k1 = θ1 exp(-θ2/ξ2) and k2 = θ3 exp(-θ4/ξ2), Eq. (2A.2), and θ1 = 5.0259 x 10^16, θ2 = 1.9279 x 10^4, θ3 = 1.3862 x 10^14, θ4 = 1.6819 x 10^4, (A.3); Figures 2.3 and 2.4 plot it as a percentage. As printed, (2A.1) divides by k1 - k2 and so is negative for all ξ: the yield of B is k1{exp(-k1 ξ1) - exp(-k2 ξ1)}/(k2 - k1). Figure 2.6 replots the contours with time on a logarithmic scale and temperature on a reciprocal scale, where a plane in R3 and a quadratic in R4 would graduate the function closely; no coefficients are printed for them, nor for the quadratic said to fit R2.

experiments.notes: The exercise defines the moments x̄ = Σx/n, c = Σx²/n and d = Σx³/n and shows that, if y = β0 + β1x + β11x² + ε is feared but the straight line is fitted, E(b0) = β0 + {(c² - x̄d)/(c - x̄²)}β11 and E(b1) = β1 + {(d - x̄c)/(c - x̄²)}β11. The answer (p. 632) applies E(b) = β + Aβ2 with A = (X'X)^-1 X'X2, X'X = [n nx̄; nx̄ nc] and X'X2 = [nc; nd]. (b) Yes: any design symmetric about zero has x̄ = d = 0, so E(b0) = β0 + cβ11 and E(b1) = β1.

experiments.title: Percentage yield of a reaction in drug manufacture: five factors in a 2^(5-1) resolution V fraction, the path of steepest ascent and its confidence cone

design.type: 2^(5-1) fractional factorial, resolution V, then points on the path of steepest ascent
design.details: I = 12345, so x5 = x1 x2 x3 x4; the amount of reagent A was kept constant; rows 17 to 20 are the points E2, E4, E6 and E8 of Table 6.4, 2, 4, 6 and 8 times the unit vector of steepest ascent rounded to two decimals

runs.notes: Rows 1 to 16 are Table 6.2 in its printed (standard, Yates) order, with run the run order; the half-effect of row 1 is printed as ȳ = 57.1750, the footnote saying 'Except for ȳ'. Rows 17 to 20 are Table 6.4, the coded and decoded conditions and observed yields of E2, E4, E6 and E8. E2 was not run: Table 6.4 prints its yield as '72.6 (run 4)', the yield of run number 4 (row 9), so y is blank in row 17.

experiments.notes: The book treats the ten two-factor interactions as error (Table 6.3), so the first-order model x1 + ... + x5 gives the standard errors; the second-degree model of the text is saturated in these 16 runs, its pure quadratic terms not estimable, so the coefficients are read from (x1 + ... + x5) ** 2. Section 6.4 reuses the first-order coefficients for a confidence cone on the direction of steepest ascent, first for x1, x2 and x3 alone (k = 3), then for all five.

experiments.title: A 3² factorial in x1 and x2 with a log response: first-, second- and third-order models, Tukey's test and confidence limits (Exercises 7.1 to 7.6)

design.details: nine runs, x1 changing fastest

runs.notes: as printed in Exercise 7.1

experiments.notes: The nine responses are y = log10 Y of runs 10 to 18 of the textile example (Table 7.1, x3 = 0). Exercise 7.2 asks for the second-order Z and Z'Z and an orthogonalized form; 7.3 the second-order fit and its analysis of variance; 7.4 Tukey's test for the first-order model; 7.5 the third-order model, which terms are estimable and the alias matrix; 7.6 confidence limits, a prediction at x1 = 0.7, x2 = 0.5 and a joint 90% region for β1 and β2. Answers, pp. 657-661: 7.1(b) judges the first-order fit good; 7.3 finds the second-order terms not significant; 7.4 finds no transformation called for; 7.5(b) says that in Z the x1³ and x2³ columns equal the x1 and x2 columns, so β111 and β222 cannot be estimated separately while β112 and β122 can; 7.5(d) explains that the alias structure alone does not say whether a coefficient can be estimated; 7.6(d) says the square of the two individual intervals would not mislead, the estimates being uncorrelated; 7.6(e) shows V(ŷ) is constant on circles.

experiments.data_source: Table 7.1 of the book (p. 212; Chapter 7, the textile experiment of Barella and Sust), in its order and with its run numbers. Table 7.1 codes x1 = (xi1 - 300)/50 (length of specimen, mm), x2 = (xi2 - 9)/1 (amplitude of load cycle, mm) and x3 = (xi3 - 45)/5 (load, g). The runs were first entered from Box and Cox (1964, Table 4); every setting and response agrees with Table 7.1. They reproduce every value of the book's S(lambda) table (p. 290) to all its digits, and its maximum 3636 and minimum 90 (p. 291). Table 7.1 also prints y = log10 Y to two decimals, which is not recorded here: the checks take logs of Y.
experiments.notes: Table 8.2 heads its values Q^2 = F - 1 (Box and Wetz's measure of estimation adequacy): F is the regression mean square over the residual mean square, the residual of the planar fit (footnote a) or of the quadratic fit (footnote b). The S(lambda) table of p. 290 is printed without units: its values are 10^-6 times the residual sum of squares of the geometric-mean scaled power of Y in cycles, so its checks read Y in thousands of cycles. Figure 8.10 plots contours of ln S(lambda1, lambda2) for the shifted power (Y + lambda2)^lambda1, reproduced from Box and Cox (1964).

factors.name: x2
factors.description: initial concentration of catalyst C; x2 = (C - 0.64)/0.20, approximately

factors.name: x3
factors.description: working pressure P; the text writes x3 = (P - 48.4)/46.2

factors.name: Block
factors.description: stage: 1 the 2^3 with five centre points, 2 the six axial runs

design.type: central composite design in two blocks
design.details: a 2^3 with five centre points (run orders 1 to 13), then six axial runs at +-1.682

runs.notes: Table E9.1 in printed order. The coded levels are approximate, as the text says: x2 = (C - 0.64)/0.20 gives 0.95 at C = 0.83 (printed 1), -1.75 at 0.29 and 1.70 at 0.98 (printed -+1.682); x1 = (T - 140)/24 gives -+1.667 at 100 and 180; and the text's x3 = (P - 48.4)/46.2 gives -0.61 and 0.62 at P = 20 and 77, not the printed -1 and 1, and 1.00 at 94.6 (printed 1.682): 46.2 is the axial half-range, so the cube levels follow (P - 48.4)/28.4, near 1.682(P - 48.4)/46.2

experiments.notes: Source: A. Coteron, N. Sanchez, M. Martinez and J. Aracil, Optimization of the synthesis of an analogue of jojoba oil using a fully central composite design, Canadian Journal of Chemical Engineering 71 (1993) 485-488. Parts (a) to (h) ask for the plane on the 13 first-stage runs, the interactions and the curvature contrast c = yf - y0 with standard deviation sigma(1/nf + 1/n0)^1/2, a second-order model with an orthogonal blocking variable placed right after the intercept, residuals, the bias under a cubic, the estimable combinations of cubic coefficients, and what to do next. Answer (pp. 680-682): the pure error SS is very small, so both the first- and second-order fits register as inadequate in a lack-of-fit test, though they explain much of the variation. (a) the plane and its analysis of variance. (b) the interactions with a common se of 1.273, said to use the 9 df residual s^2 = 4.723^2, and 0.301 with s from pure error (1.273 is the se of a fit of the plane and the three interactions, whose residual has 6 df and s = 3.601; s = 4.723 gives 4.723/8^1/2 = 1.670, and the pure-error s = 1.118 gives 0.395); the curvature contrast c = 30.5 - 28.2 = 2.3, 3.61 times its se of 0.637, so a second-order model seems needed. (c) a blocking variable B = 1 for run orders 1-13 and B2 = -1.4138652 for 14-19 makes the blocks orthogonal to every column but the 1's; the second-order terms take about 62% of what first order leaves. (d) the residuals show nothing startling, but the 18 residuals share only 8 df. (e) the alias matrix: E(b_i) = beta_i + 0.58572676(3 beta_iii + beta_ijj + beta_ill), all other estimates unbiased. (f) Z2.1 has four independent columns, three in the cubic betas of (e) with different coefficients and one in beta123 alone; their 1 df sums of squares add to the lack of fit of (c) because the contrasts are orthogonal. (g) none. (h) a plot or contours of y-hat against temperature and pressure, or a ridge analysis from the coded origin (Section 12.7).

experiments.title: Hoerl's saddle in two factors: the ridge of maximum response from the origin, and the four stationary paths

where.section: 12.3, Worked Example of Ridge Analysis about the Origin x = 0
tables: Unnumbered table of lambda, x1, x2, R and y-hat on p. 395

design.details: A. E. Hoerl's (1959) surface in two coded factors, a saddle; b0 = 80, b = (0.1, 0.2)', B = [0.2 0.5; 0.5 0.1]

experiments.data_source: none: the example starts from the fitted equation y-hat = 80 + 0.1x1 + 0.2x2 + 0.2x1^2 + 0.1x2^2 + x1x2, Eq. (12.3.1), printed without the data it was fitted to. The eigenvalues, the stationary point and the path of maximum response are checked through the library's optimize_responses on these coefficients; each row of the table is compared with the library's ridge on the sphere of the printed radius R.
experiments.notes: The table on p. 395 does not follow Eq. (12.3.4), x = -(1/2)(B - lambda I)^-1 b, from which the text says it comes: at every printed lambda its x1 and x2 are twice what (12.3.4) gives (at lambda = 0.80, (12.3.4) gives (0.50, 0.50); the table prints (1.00, 1.00)), as if the factor 1/2 were dropped, and R and y-hat are then worked at those doubled points. The doubled points are near, but not on, the path of maximum y-hat of (12.3.1), and the printed lambda is not its multiplier at the printed R. The point for lambda = 0.2 on p. 396 and the focus table on p. 400 do follow (12.2.8) and (12.4.5). The text on p. 395 says curves 3 and 4 come from lambda between the eigenvalues; it is curves 2 and 3 (Figure 12.2's caption). Exercise 12.5 asks for paths 2, 3 and 4.

experiments.name: box-draper-12-exercise-12-4-wheat-gluten-films
experiments.title: Exercise 12.4: six properties of edible wheat gluten films against gluten, ethanol and pH in a central composite design

design.details: a 2^3 with six axial runs at 2 and four centre runs (runs 1 to 18), then run 19, a verification point at (1, 0, -1)

runs.notes: Table E12.4 in printed order. Run 19 is the verification point, made after the initial response surface analysis; the line below it, the values predicted at (1, 0, -1), is in expected.

experiments.notes: Source: N. Gontard, S. Guilbert and J. L. Cuq, Journal of Food Science 57(1), 1992, 190-195, 199. The units of the responses are in the source paper. The full quadratic fitted to runs 1 to 18 predicts 32.32, 35.39, 0.922, 2.61, 9.14 and 0.763 at (1, 0, -1), with or without x1x2x3; no subset of the quadratic's terms gives the printed 30.1, 35.3, 2.56 together. Answer (pp. 711-712): Table E12.4a's coefficients are those of the full quadratic plus x1x2x3 fitted to runs 1 to 18; x1x2x3 is orthogonal to the other columns, so adding or dropping it changes no other estimate. Table E12.4b's verdicts (lack of fit; significant regression at 0.05 using the residual mean square): y1 quadratic Yes/No, cubic Yes/No; y2 Yes/Yes, Yes/Yes; y3 No/No, No/Borderline; y4 in x1 only No/Yes (with a non-normal residual plot), quadratic Yes/No, cubic Yes/Yes; y5 Yes/No, Yes/No; y6 Yes/Yes, Yes/No. For y4 only x1 and x1^2 are individually significant in the full regression; Tables E12.4c and E12.4d give the ridge paths of the quadratic in x1 alone and of the full quadratic, and the answer concludes that x2 and x3 contribute little. experiments.title: Exercise 12.10: NBS abrasion resistance of a rubber compound in a three-factor composite design

design.details: a 2^3 cube, six axial runs at 2 and one centre run

runs.notes: Table E12.10 in printed order, adapted by the book from Figure 5, p. 80, of the source paper

experiments.notes: Source: J. R. Carney and R. W. Hallman, Rubber World, September 1967, 78-83. The exercise asks where, on or within a sphere of radius 2, the highest abrasion resistance is predicted. Answer (pp. 718-720): the eigenvalues -3.64, -0.66, 3.14 put the maximum path at lambda > 3.14; within a sphere of radius 2 an optimum of about 60.5 is predicted. The ridge checks take the fitted equation as printed (b11 = -0.285); its restatement as b and B prints b1 = -6.902 and B[1,1] = 0.285. The answer's eigenvalues (-3.64, -0.66, 3.14) and its path table do not follow the printed surface (eigenvalues -3.550, -0.561, 3.481; at R = 2 the maximum is 61.64 at (-1.296, -0.075, 1.521), lambda = 5.50) nor its b and B form with B[1,1] = +0.285: they follow a surface with b33 near 1.17 in place of 1.690 (b33 = 1.17 gives eigenvalues -3.638, -0.656, 3.143 and reproduces the path to within a unit in the last printed digit). Figure E12.10 reproduces the source paper's contour slices; the book's data were made by adding random normal errors to fitted values read at the composite design's points.

experiments.name: box-draper-12-exercise-12-11-hearts-of-palm
experiments.title: Exercise 12.11: viscosity of foliole puree of hearts of palm after cellulase and pectinase treatments

design.details: a 2^3 cube, axial runs at 3^1/2 = 1.732 for x1 and x2 and at 1 for x3, and five centre points

runs.notes: Table E12.11a in printed order; the axial distance printed 1.732 is 3^1/2

experiments.notes: Source: R. Kitagawa, R. E. Bruns and T. J. B. De Menezes, Journal of Food Science 59(4), 1994, 844-848. Lower viscosities are better. Answer (pp. 720-721): lower responses are wanted, so both paths are paths of minimum response (lambda below the smallest eigenvalue); E = 0.75 + 0.25x1, t = 5 + x2, T = 45 + 5x3 uncode the points. The answer notes that its first response agrees well with the paper, while for the second there are unresolved differences. The coefficient checks fit the settings as printed, 1.732 (the fit to 3^1/2 moves B[1,1] to 12.809, B[2,2] to 12.142 and B[3,3] to -3.470). The second response's b prints b2 = -6.984, but the fit gives -6.948 and Table E12.11c follows -6.948 (at lambda = -12 it gives (1.468, 1.138, -0.231), R = 1.872, y-hat = 30.60; -6.984 gives (1.470, 1.140, -0.231), 1.874, 30.44), so the ridge and eigenvalue checks of y2 take b2 = -6.948. The two R^2 are swapped: the fits give 0.900 for y1 and 0.910 for y2. experiments.title: Exercise 12.12: tensile strength of silica filled natural rubber in a third-order rotatable design in three blocks

factors.name: B1

factors.name: B2
factors.description: block variable B2 (1, -2, 1 for blocks 1, 2, 3), entered by its printed values

design.type: third-order rotatable design in three blocks
design.details: block 1 a 2^2 with three centre points, block 2 four axial points at 1.414 with three centre points, block 3 seven points on a circle of radius 1.069; block variables B1 and B2

runs.notes: Table E12.12a in printed order; B1 and B2 are the block variables, listed as categorical factors with coding none so that a model carries them by their printed values; they are not treatment factors

experiments.notes: Source: G. C. Derringer, a presentation to the American Chemical Society, Division of Rubber Chemistry, 1969. Block 3's points are 1.069(cos 2 pi j/7, sin 2 pi j/7) printed to three decimals. Answer (pp. 721-724): the block variables enter right after the constant, as a different mean level for each block; lack of fit is not significant, so the other F tests use s^2 = 7880 on 9 df, and the third-order terms are judged worth including. Figures E12.12a and b contour the quadratic and cubic fits: their regions of high tensile strength (the closed 3800 contours) overlap, but the cubic's open 3800 contour contradicts the quadratic. Table E12.12b adds five more responses for the same 21 runs (300% modulus, 500% modulus, elongation at break, Mooney scorch, 95% rheometer cure time; desirable: high, high, low, high, low), as data for further exercises with no answers; they are not recorded here. The fit is to the settings as printed (1.414). The lack-of-fit and pure-error mean squares are printed equal to their sums of squares (51,851 and 19,067, not 10,370 and 4,767), and the lack-of-fit F 2.72 is 51,851/19,067; on 5 and 4 df it is 2.18. The other F ratios divide by s^2 rounded to 7880. Check choices: B1 and B2 are listed as factors, typed categorical with coding none, because a model can only carry columns that are factors and the answer's cubic includes the block variables by their printed values; typed numeric they would enter run_radius and move the block-3 radius checks. The fits use the settings as printed (1.414), as the answer's coefficients do.

experiments.title: Exercise 12.1: a two-factor quadratic whose ridge radius stays finite at an eigenvalue, the answer's example

design.details: the answer's numerical example: b1 = 2^1/2 - 1, b2 = 1, b11 = 1, b22 = 3, b12 = 2 (b0 not given)

experiments.data_source: none: the exercise asks to show that if b22 - b2 b12/(2b1) = b11 - b1 b12/(2b2) equals an eigenvalue of B, R in Eq. (12.2.4) does not go to infinity at that eigenvalue; the answer gives the surface y-hat = b0 + (2^1/2 - 1)x1 + x2 + x1^2 + 3x2^2 + 2x1x2 as an example.
experiments.notes: The answer says to write out x from (12.2.8): the factor (lambda - lambda_i) appears top and bottom and cancels, det(B - lambda I) being (lambda - lambda1)(lambda - lambda2). It adds that such a case is very unlikely in practice, and cites Fan (1999).

check.manual: a coefficient of the answer's constructed surface, an input, not a result. With B = [1 1; 1 3] (b12/2 off the diagonal) the eigenvalues are 2 -/+ 2^1/2, and b22 - b2 b12/(2b1) = b11 - b1 b12/(2b2) = 2 - 2^1/2, the smaller: b = (2^1/2 - 1, 1)' lies along the eigenvector of 2 + 2^1/2, so the factor (lambda - (2 - 2^1/2)) cancels and R stays finite (0.1913) as lambda tends to it (worked with numpy); the library reports eigenvalues but has no test of this condition, and the answer prints no result to compare

experiments.title: Exercise 12.8: ridge path of maximum yield of lettuce tops for Exercise 11.22's surface (source 1)

responses.name: y
responses.description: yield of tops with NO3- and Fe2+ (source 1 of Exercise 11.22)

design.details: Exercise 11.22's 2^3 with six axial runs at 1.68 and six centre runs, the lower cube level of x3 run at -0.5

runs.notes: Table E11.22b (Chapter 11, pp. 385-387), source 1, in printed order; the other three sources are not used here

experiments.data_source: Exercise 11.22's data, printed in Chapter 11. The answer does not print its surface; the least-squares full quadratic in (x1, x2, x3) fitted to source 1 reproduces its y-hat at the origin, 18.726, and its stationary point (-0.751, -0.041, -0.292), y-hat 21.261, so source 1 is the surface used. The checks pass that fit's coefficients, rounded to four decimals, to optimize_responses: b0 = 18.7262, b = (-6.2345, -0.2158, -1.2997)', b11 = -4.5741, b22 = -0.6130, b33 = -5.2756, b12 = -0.7938, b13 = 2.2868, b23 = 1.4773. The answer works from these rounded values: they give its eigenvalues -3.73308 and -0.48633 (the unrounded fit gives -3.73310 and -0.48628) and its y-hat of -74.69 at R = 14.111 (unrounded, -74.68).
experiments.notes: Answer (pp. 715-716): (a) for the maximum path lambda runs from infinity down to the largest eigenvalue -0.48633, x = -(1/2)(B - lambda I)^-1 b, R = (x'x)^1/2, y-hat = b0 + x'b + x'Bx; the path passes through the stationary point (lambda = 0) and then declines, going negative below lambda = -0.45 (an extrapolation of no practical use). (b) with spheres about the stationary point f = x_S the solution stays at x = x_S for any lambda that is not an eigenvalue, since 2(B - lambda I)x = -b - 2 lambda x_S reduces to 2(B - lambda I)x_S. The note after Table E12.8 about x4 belongs to Exercise 12.7. Rows lambda = -0.4 and -0.48 print R^2 for R. Check choice: the ridge and eigenvalue checks take the least-squares fit's coefficients rounded to four decimals, because they reproduce the answer's eigenvalues -3.73308 and -0.48633 and its y-hat of -74.69 at R = 14.111, which the unrounded fit misses (-3.73310, -0.48628, -74.68).

experiments.name: box-draper-18-exercise-18-1-tablet-dissolution
experiments.title: Dissolution of 14 tablet blends of binder, disintegrant, surfactant and other ingredients: a Scheffé quadratic and a component-amount fit (Exercise 18.1; Cornell and Gorman 2003)

design.details: x1, x2 and x3 small percentages, x4 the rest of the 100; blends 4 and 8, and 5 and 11, are replicates

runs.notes: Table E18.1 in its printed order with its fitted values ŷ; the summary rows (Min., Max, Average, Range) are recorded as expected numbers

experiments.notes: Fits (a) and (b) give the same fitted values to 13 digits, and these reproduce the printed ŷ (verified while cataloguing). In fit (a), with the percentages as printed, x3's coefficient is about -30,930, the very large coefficient the exercise points to. The summary row's average of x4, 96.170, is 96.172 from the column, and its range 1.300 is half of 97.500 - 94.900 = 2.600. The book's answer (pp. 734-735) prints both fits' coefficient tables and ANOVAs; all its numbers are recorded. In words it adds that the fitted values are the same for both equations and are the last column of Table E18.1, and that fit (b) could instead be fitted to shifted and scaled amounts, u_i = {a_i - min(a_i)}/range(a_i), which run from 0 to 1, so that the coefficients have a simple interpretation. Fit (a)'s ANOVA is about zero: its regression and total sums of squares (1124.33 and 1125.18 on 10 and 14 df) are uncorrected, while fit (b)'s are about the mean (68.7374 and 69.5835 on 9 and 13 df); the residual, lack-of-fit and pure-error rows are the same in both.

factors.name: x1
factors.description: polyethylene glycol 400 (the table's heading spells it Polyethelyne)

design.type: extreme vertices mixture design (McLean and Anderson 1966) on a region cut by component bounds
design.details: two true vertices, four averages of close pairs of true vertices, five edge or face centroids and the overall centroid; x5 held at 0.10 so x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 = 0.9

runs.notes: Table 19.1, its rows in printed order; the rows of lower and upper limits are the factors' low and high. x1 + x2 + x3 + x4 = 0.9 at every run, the fifth ingredient x5 being held at 0.10. Runs 3 to 6 are each the average of two close true vertices (p. 598), which the authors called vertices.

experiments.notes: Anik and Sukumar (1981). The Scheffé quadratic model is fitted without x2x4, which the design makes linearly dependent on the other columns (Eq. 19.2.5). Three sets of ridge paths follow: under the mixture restriction alone (Table 19.2), on the face x3 = 0.08 (Table 19.3) and on the edge x3 = 0.08, x4 = 0.30 (Table 19.4). The book rounds each ridge point's coordinates so that they sum to 0.900. Figure 19.2 plots path A of Table 19.2 and Figure 19.3 the paths of Table 19.3 over contours of Eq. 19.2.4. Appendix 19B lists the MINITAB macro used; its data lines repeat b, f, B, A, c and T of Eqs. 19.5.2 to 19.5.5, with k2 = 50 the λ of the call shown.
